The system described in this section accounts for only the most common stem shapes. 1.4.1. Primary stress can fall on either the root or a suffix; prefixes are always unstressed. Three types of roots with respect to underlying stress properties can be recognized: strong, weak, and vowelless. Similarly there are four types of suffixes: strong, ambivalent, weak, and unstressed. Strong roots tend to attract stress, losing it only to strong suffixes. ... Weak roots lose stress to both strong and ambivalent suffixes. ... Weak suffixes are stressed only when following vowelless roots. ... The fourth type of suffix is never stressed. ... 2) There is a tendency to penultimate stress. sweep_summary: Only one sweep item: Leonard 2006, 'Formalising stress in SENĆOŦEN' (UVic MA thesis, 108 pp), already in our bibliography. The thesis PDF could not be obtained (UVicSpace hdl 1828/2105 returns 403 to this host on every endpoint; the 2019 Wayback snapshot is unreachable; scholarly APIs rate-limited), but its full abstract was read from the UVic catalogue record (saved) and its published revised version, Leonard 2007 NWJL 1.4 (on file from the 2026-09-16 audit), was read in full. Both argue that stress in SENĆOŦEN lexical stems is largely phonological — right-aligned trochaic (penultimate tendency) with weight sensitivity (full vowel over schwa) — and that much of Montler 1986's morpho-lexical root/suffix hierarchy is unnecessary, while conceding a residue of unpredictable cases and a scope limited to disyllabic roots and lexical-suffix stems. This refines rather than overturns the catalog's 'morphological' coding, which rests on Montler 1986 (the reference grammar by the principal field linguist) and is still echoed by Montler's 2025 online grammar ('stress is not completely predictable'; on file). Recommend keeping Montler 1986 as deciding source and adding a note that Leonard 2006/2007 reanalyses most lexical-stem stress as a weight-sensitive right-aligned trochee with residual lexical exceptions. Acquiring the thesis itself is low priority since its published revision is held. written at

new_statements.quote: In this paper, I support both Montler (1986:23) and Kiyota (2003:7) in their first claim, that stress tends to be penultimate. However, my research does not support their second claim, that stress in SENĆOŦEN is a morphologically complex system. Instead, I argue that the stress pattern of many SENĆOŦEN lexical stems can be accounted for by assuming that left-headed binary feet are aligned to the right edge of a lexical stem and that SENĆOŦEN is sensitive to the phonological weight distinction between full vowel and schwa.

new_statements.locator: p. 2, sec. 1 Introduction (same claim restated p. 30 sec. 4.1 and pp. 53-54 sec. 5)
new_statements.reading: Leonard reanalyses the SENĆOŦEN stress pattern that Montler 1986 describes as a morpho-lexical hierarchy (strong/weak/vowelless roots vs strong/ambivalent/weak/unstressed suffixes) as mostly phonological: a right-aligned trochee (penultimate default) overridden by weight, full vowel > schwa. She restricts the claim to disyllabic roots and root+lexical-suffix stems, explicitly leaves a residue of unpredictable, lexically specified cases (p. 30; fn 18; ex. 7b), and calls the account preliminary. This is the only dedicated stress study of the language and it is first-hand (fieldwork plus Montler's published data).

sources.quote: 'Stressed vowels are produced a little louder, longer, and stronger than other vowels in the word. ... In the SENĆOŦEN alphabet, stress is also not marked, but the situation is not as difficult as for English. In general, if there is one A, Á, I, O, or U in the word, that one is the stressed vowel. ... If the word has only E vowels, it is often a good guess to stress the second E from the end. ... sources.quote: Montler (1986: 23) states that in SENCOTEN, roots and affixes are lexically specified for their stress properties. He claims that these roots and affixes are in a hierarchical relationship and compete with each other for stress assignment. However, in this thesis, I show that there is much less morpho-lexical stress in SENCOTEN than previously thought. ... I show that it is the weight distinction between full vowels and schwa that determines where stress will be assigned. In addition, I am able to show that metrical feet are grouped into trochees and that these trochaic feet are aligned to the right edge of the word.
